editorialDecl.p: EEBO-TCP is a partnership between the Universities of Michigan and Oxford and the publisher ProQuest to create accurately transcribed and encoded texts based on the image sets published by ProQuest via their Early English Books Online (EEBO) database (http://eebo.chadwyck.com). The general aim of EEBO-TCP is to encode one copy (usually the first edition) of every monographic English-language title published between 1473 and 1700 available in EEBO.

EEBO-TCP aimed to produce large quantities of textual data within the usual project restraints of time and funding, and therefore chose to create diplomatic transcriptions (as opposed to critical editions) with light-touch, mainly structural encoding based on the Text Encoding Initiative (http://www.tei-c.org).

The EEBO-TCP project was divided into two phases. The 25,363 texts created during Phase 1 of the project have been released into the public domain as of 1 January 2015. Anyone can now take and use these texts for their own purposes, but we respectfully request that due credit and attribution is given to their original source.
Users should be aware of the process of creating the TCP texts, and therefore of any assumptions that can be made about the data.

Text selection was based on the New Cambridge Bibliography of English Literature (NCBEL). If an author (or for an anonymous work, the title) appears in NCBEL, then their works are eligible for inclusion. Selection was intended to range over a wide variety of subject areas, to reflect the true nature of the print record of the period. In general, first editions of a works in English were prioritized, although there are a number of works in other languages, notably Latin and Welsh, included and sometimes a second or later edition of a work was chosen if there was a compelling reason to do so.

Image sets were sent to external keying companies for transcription and basic encoding. Quality assurance was then carried out by editorial teams in Oxford and Michigan. 5% (or 5 pages, whichever is the greater) of each text was proofread for accuracy and those which did not meet QA standards were returned to the keyers to be redone. After proofreading, the encoding was enhanced and/or corrected and characters marked as illegible were corrected where possible up to a limit of 100 instances per text. Any remaining illegibles were encoded as <gap>s. Understanding these processes should make clear that, while the overall quality of TCP data is very good, some errors will remain and some readable characters will be marked as illegible. Users should bear in mind that in all likelihood such instances will never have been looked at by a TCP editor.
The texts were encoded and linked to page images in accordance with level 4 of the TEI in Libraries guidelines.

Copies of the texts have been issued variously as SGML (TCP schema; ASCII text with mnemonic sdata character entities); displayable XML (TCP schema; characters represented either as UTF-8 Unicode or text strings within braces); or lossless XML (TEI P5, characters represented either as UTF-8 Unicode or TEI g elements).
Keying and markup guidelines are available at the Text Creation Partnership web site.
This file is the EEBO-TCP transcription with editorial layers added inline; nothing of the transcription has been removed.

choice/orig holds the text as printed; choice/reg holds the modern reading. reg/@resp says who decided it (#auto = machine, #editor = reviewed by hand); reg/@type is spelling, case, punctuation, spacing, grammar (an archaic form modernized: thou, hath, -eth), reference (a scripture reference in the modern style: Heb. xii. 5 as Heb 12:5) or emendation (another word, or a word added or removed). Where the editor overrode the machine, the editor's reg comes first and the machine's proposal follows as a second reg[@resp='#auto'].
choice/abbr + choice/expan: macron abbreviations (e.g. frō = from) and superscript contractions (yᵉ = the).
supplied: letters or words lost to illegible print, with @cert and a comment giving the evidence; the TCP gap element is kept inside.

Spelling regularized: u/v, i/j, silent final e, doubled consonants, -ie to -y, -nesse to -ness, and a word list. Grammatical forms (hath, doth, thou, thee, thy, ye, shalt, wilt, art, hast, dost) are retained. Footnote text is left in original spelling.
list[@change='#review']: run-in enumerations (I. ... II. ...) set out as numbered lists; the printed numerals are kept in label.
head[@type='edition']: section title used by this edition; the printed heading is kept in the preceding head. @change='#review' points at the revisionDesc entry for these structural changes.
Line breaks are those of the TCP transcription (newlines in the text; g[@ref='char:EOLhyphen'] marks a word hyphenated at line end). pb/@n is the printed page, pb/@facs the page image.

div.p: A Divinedivine and Supernaturalsupernatural LIGHTlight, Immediatelyimmediately imparted to the Soulsoul by the SPIRIT of GOD, Shown to be both a Scriptural, and Rational DOCTRINEdoctrine; Inin a SERMONsermon Preach'd at Northampton. And Published at the Desiredesire of some of the Hearershearers.
By Jonathan Edwards, A. M. Pastor of the Churchchurch there.

q.p: —Whence the • cometh wisdom? andAnd where is the place of understanding?
Look ye blind that ye may see.
—Until the day dawn and the day-star arise in your hearts.

div.p: BOSTON: Printed by S. KNEELAND and T. GREEN.
M, DCC, XXXIV.

div.head: The PREFACE.
div.p:
I Am •• am sensible that m • y con • sent • ing that the fol • lowing Discoursediscourse of mine should 〈…〉 be published, n • eeds Excuseexcuse; but yet I don't 〈◊〉 think it with the while for m • e, much 〈◊〉 to excuse my self, by declaring how backward I was to is, and how much • I was urged, and that I was prevailed 〈◊〉 with to do it, more to gratify others▪ and with an aim 〈…〉 at promoting the Interestinterest of Religion • religion▪ and the Goodgood of Soulssouls, than by any thought I had of any Honourhonour that I should get by it: for such things, I believe 〈…〉 , ordinarily make less Impressionimpression upon the R • eaders, to alter their thought of the Authorauthor, and his Design 〈◊〉 design, than the Authorsauthors generally think for. They at whose desire, and upon whose Accountaccount chiefly, this Sermonsermon is • printed, are already acquainted with the Circumstancescircumstances of the Mattermatter; and if any others should happen to see it, and should think it worth their while to read it • , I shall only desire of them, that they would put as favourable a Constructionconstruction u • pon my herein appearing in Print, as they can; and that they would read the following Discoursediscourse with Candou • r, and without Prejudiceprejudice against it, either from an Ideaidea of the Author's Forwardnessforwardness and Ostentationostentation, or the Unfashionableness of the Subjectsubject. As to you, that are the Peoplepeople of the Fl • ockflock, of which CHRIST hath called me to the Oversight, I have no Reasonreason to be jealous that you will have any
Prejudiceprejudice against this Discoursediscourse, upon either of these mention'd Accountsaccounts, to stand in the way of your duly weighing, and considering, and suitably entertaining the things treated of in it. I have Reasonreason to bless GOD, that there is a more happy Unionunion between us, than that you should be prejudiced against any thing of mine, because 'tis mine; Andand however the subject is out of Mo • de in the Worldworld, 'tis doubtless your peculiar Happinesshappiness, that you have been so thoroughly instructed in such like Doctrinesdoctrines, even from your Beginningbeginning: and I rejoice in it, that Providenceprovidence, in this Dayday of Corruptioncorruption and Confusionconfusion, has cast my Lot • where such Doctrinesdoctrines, that I look upon so much the Lifelife and Gloryglory of the Gospelgospel, are not only ow • n'd, but where there are so many, in whom the Truthtruth of them is so apparently manifest, in their Experienceexperience, that any one who has had the Opportunityopportunity of Acquaintanceacquaintance with them in such matters, that • I have had, must be very unreasonable to doubt of it. It is pleasant to me to read discourses on such Subjectssubjects, and to see such Doctrinesdoctrines well treated of in Booksbooks, but much more pleasant, to see them clearly exemplified. If what is here offered to you▪ shall be a means further to establish you in such Truthstruths, and to make those among you, that yet remain in spiritual Darknessdarkness and Blindnessblindness, sensible of their Miserymisery, and stir them up earnestly to seek after this spiritual and divine Illuminationillumination; and shall be for the Comfortcomfort and Edification of those that have Experienced it, I shall have great Reasonreason to rejoice, and be thankful: and I desire your earnest and continual Prayersprayers for me, that I may be the Instrumentinstrument of much such Goodgood to you, and Gloryglory to GOD therein.

div.head: THE Reality of Spiritual Light.

q.p: And JESUS answered and said unto him, blessed art thou Simon Barjona; for Fleshflesh and Bloodblood hath not revealed it unto thee, but my Father which is in Heavenheaven.

div.p:
CHRISTChrist says these Wordswords to Peter, upon Occasionoccasion of his professing his Faithfaith in him as the Son of GOD. Our Lord was enquiring of his Disciplesdisciples, who Menmen said he was; not that he needed to be informed, but only to introduce and give Occasionoccasion to what follows. They answer, that some said he was John the Baptist, and some Elias, and others Jeremias or one of the Prophetsprophets. When they had 〈◊〉 t • hus given an Accountaccount, who others said he 〈◊〉 was, CHRIST asks them, who they said he 〈◊〉 was. Simon Peter, whom we find always
zealous and forward, was the first to answer; be readily replied to the Questionquestion, Thou art CHRIST the Son of the living GOD.
UPON this Occasionoccasion CHRIST says as he does to him and of him in the Texttext: Inin which we may observe,

1. THAT Peter is pronounced blessed on this Accountaccount. Blessed art thou — Thouthou art an happy man, that thou art not ignorant of this, that I am CHRIST the Son of the living GOD. Thou art distinguishingly happy. Others are blinded, and have dark and deluded Apprehensionsapprehensions, as you have now given an Accountaccount, some thinking that I am Elias, and some that I am Jeremias, and some one thing, and some another; but none of them thinking right, all of them misled. Happy art thou, that art so distinguished as to know the Truthtruth in this Mattermatter.
2. THE Evidenceevidence of this his Happinesshappiness declared; viz. That GOD and he only had revealed it to him. This is an Evidenceevidence of his being blessed.

First, ASas it shows how peculiarly favoured he was of GOD, above others. qQ. dD. How highly favoured art thou, that others that are wise and great Menmen, the Scribes, Phar • isees, and Rulersrulers, and the Nationnation in general, are left in Darknessdarkness, to follow their own misguided Apprehensionsapprehensions, and that thou should'st be singled out, as it were by Namename, that my heavenly Father should thus set his Lovelove on thee Simon 〈◊〉 Bar-jonaiona. This argues thee blessed, that thou should'st thus be the Objectobject of GOD'sGod's distinguishing Lovelove.

Secondly, ITit evidences his Blessednessblessedness also, as it intimates that this Knowlege is above any that Fleshflesh and Bloodblood can reveal. This is such Knowlege as my Father which in Heavenheaven only can give: Itit is too high and excellent to be communicated by such Meansmeans as other Knowlege is. Thou art blessed, that thou knowest that which GOD alone can teach thee.

THE Originaloriginal of this Knowlege is here declared; both negatively and positively. Positively, as GOD is here declared the Authorauthor of it. Negatively, as 'tis declared that Fleshflesh and Bloodblood had not revealed it. GOD is the Authorauthor of all Knowlege and Understandingunderstanding whatsoever: Hehe is the Authorauthor of the Knowledgeknowledge, that is obtained by human Learninglearning: Hehe is the Authorauthor of all moral Prudence, and of the Knowlege and Skillskill that Menmen have in their secular Businessbusiness. Thus it is said of all in Israel that were wise-hearted, and skill'd in Embroidering, that GOD had fill'd them with the spirit of Wisdo • mwisdom. Exod. 28.3.

GOD is the Authorauthor of such Knowlege; but yet not so but that Fleshflesh and Bloodblood reveals it. Mortal Menmen are capable of imparting the Knowlege of human Artsarts and Sciences, and Skillskill in temporal Affairsaffairs. GOD is the Authorauthor of such Knowlege by those Meansmeans: Fleshflesh and Bloodblood is made use of by GOD as the mediate or second Causecause of it; Hehe conveys it by the Powerpower and Influenceinfluence of natural Meansmeans. But this spiritual Knowlege, spoken of in the Texttext, is what GOD is the Authorauthor of, and none else: Hehe reveals it and Flesh and Bloodblood reveals
it not. He imparts this Knowlege immediately, not making use of any intermediate natural Causescauses, as he does in other Knowlege.

WHAT had passed in the preceeding Discoursediscourse, naturally occasioned CHRIST to observe this▪ because the Disciplesdisciples had been telling, how others did not know him, but were generally mistaken about him, and divided and confounded in their Opinionsopinions of him: but Peter had declared his assured Faithfaith that he was the Son of GOD. Now it was natural to observe, how it was not Fleshflesh and Bloodblood, that had revealed it to him, but GOD; for if this knowlege were dependent on natural Causescauses or Meansmeans, how came it to pass that they, a Companycompany of poor Fishermen, illiterate Menmen, and Personspersons of low Educationeducation, attain'd to the knowlege of the Truthtruth; while the Scribes and Pharisees, Menmen of vastly higher advantages, and greater knowlege and sagacity in other matters, remain'd in Ignoranceignorance? This could be owing only to the gracious distinguishing Influenceinfluence and Revelationrevelation of the SPIRIT of GOD. Hence, what I would make the Subjectsubject of my present Discoursediscourse from these Wordswords, is this

q.p: DOCTRINE, viz. That there is such a thing, as A SPIRITUALspiritual and DIVINEdivine LIGHTlight, immediately imparted to the So • ulsoul by GOD, of a different Naturenature from any that is obtain'd by natural Meansmeans.

div.p: IN what I say on this Subjectsubject at this Timetime, would
I. SHOW what this divine Lightlight is.
II. HOW it is given Immediatelyimmediately by GOD, and not obtain'd by natural Meansmeans.
III. SHOW the Truthtruth of the Doctrinedoctrine.
AND then conclude with a brief Improvementimprovement.
1. I would show what this spiritual and divine Lightlight is. And in order to it would shewshow,
First, INin a few things what it is not. And here,

1. THOSE Convictionsconvictions that natural Menmen may have of their Sinsin and Miserymisery is not this spiritual and divine Lightlight. Men in a natural Conditioncondition may have Convictionsconvictions of the Guiltguilt that lies upon them, and of the anger of GOD, and their Dangerdanger of divine Vengeancevengeance. Such Convictionsconvictions are from Lightlight or Sensiblenesssensibleness of Truthtruth: that some Sinnerssinners have a greater Convictionconviction of their Guiltguilt and Miserymisery than others, is because some have more Lightlight, or more of an Apprehensionapprehension of Truthtruth, than others. And this Lightlight and Convictionconviction may be from the Spirit of GOD; the SPIRIT convinces Menmen of Sinsin: but yet nature is much more concern'd in it than in the Communicationcommunication of that spiritual and divine Lightlight, that is spoken of in the Doctrinedoctrine; 'tis from the Spirit of GOD only as assisting natural Principlesprinciples, and not as
infusing any new Principlesprinciples. Common Gracegrace differs from special, in that it influences only by assisting of Naturenature; and not • by imparting Gracegrace, or bestowing any thing above Naturenature. The Lightlight that is obtain'd, is wholly natural, or of no superioursuperior Kindkind to what meer Naturenature attains to; tho' more of that kind be obtained, than would be obtained if Menmen were left wholly to themselves. Or in other Wordswords, Common Gracegrace only assists the Facultiesfaculties of the Soulsoul to do that more fully, which they do by Naturenature; as natural Conscienceconscience, or Reasonreason, will by meer Naturenature make a Manman sensible of Guiltguilt, and will accuse and condemn him when he has done amiss. Conscience is a Principleprinciple natural to Menmen; and the Workwork that it doth naturally, or of it self, is to give an Apprehensionapprehension of right and wrong; and to suggest to the Mindmind the Relationrelation that there is between right and wrong, and a Retributionretribution. The Spirit of GOD, in those Convictionsconvictions which unregenerate Menmen sometimes have, assists Conscienceconscience to do this Workwork in a further Degreedegree, than it would do if they were left to themselves: Hehe helps it against those Thingsthings that tend to stupify it, and obstruct its Exerciseexercise. But in the renewing and sanctifying work of the HOLYholy GHOST, those things are wrought in the Soulsoul that are above Naturenature; and of which ther • e is nothing of the like kind in the Soulsoul by Naturenature▪ and they are caused to exist in the Soulsoul habit •••• ually, & according to such a stated Constitutionconstitution or Lawlaw, that lays such a Foundationfoundation for Exer ••• cisesexercises in a continued Coursecourse, as is called a Principle 〈◊〉 principle of nature. Not only are remaini • ng Principles ••• principles
assisted 〈…〉 to do their work more freely and fully, 〈…〉 but those Principlesprinciples are restored that were utterly destroyed by the
Fallfall; and the mind thence-forward habitually exerts those acts that the Dominiondominion of Sinsin had made it as wholly destitute of, as a dead Bodybody is of vital Acts.

THE Spirit of GOD acts in a very different manner in the one Casecase, from what he doth in the other. He may indeed act upon the Mindmind of a natural Manman; but he acts in the Mindmind of a Saintsaint as an indwelling vital Principleprinciple. He acts upon the Mindmind of an unregenerate Personperson as an extrinsick occasional Agentagent; for in acting upon them he doth not unite himself to them; for notwithstanding all his Influencesinfluences that they may be the Subjectssubjects of, they a • re still sensual having not the Spirit. Jude 19. •• ▪ Butbut he unites himself with the Mindmind of a Saint •• saint, takes him for his Templetemple, actuates and influences him as a new, supernatural Principleprinciple of Lifelife and Actionaction. There is this Differencedifference; that the Spirit of GOD in acting in the Soulsoul of a Godlygodly Manman, exerts and communicates himself there in his own proper Naturenature. Holiness is the proper Naturenature of the Spirit of GOD. The HOLYholy SPIRIT operates in the Mindsminds of the Godlygodly, by uniting himself to them, and living in them, and exerting his own Naturenature in the Exerciseexercise of their Facultiesfaculties. The Spirit of GOD may act upon a Creaturecreature, and yet not, in acting communicate himself. The Spirit of GOD may act upon inanimate Creaturescreatures; as the Spirit moved upon the Faceface of the Waterswaters, in the Beginningbeginning of the Creationcreation: Soso the Spirit of GOD may act upon the minds of Menmen, many ways, and communicate himself no more than when he acts upon an inanimate Creaturecreature. For Instanceinstance. He may excite Thoughtsthoughts in them, may assist
their natural Reasonreason and Understandingunderstanding, or may assist other natural Principlesprinciples, and this without any Unionunion with the Soulsoul, but may act, as it were, as upon an external Objectobject. But as he acts in his holy Influencesinfluences, and spiritual Operationsoperations, he acts in a way of peculiar Communicationcommunication of himself; so that the Subjectsubject is thence denominated Spiritualspiritual.

2 THIS spiritual and divine Lightlight don't consist in any Impressionimpression made upon the Imaginationimagination. 'Tis no Impressionimpression upon the Mindmind, as tho' one saw any thing with the bodily Eyeseyes: 'Tis'tis no Imaginationimagination or Ideaidea of an outward Lightlight or Gloryglory, or any Beautybeauty of Formform or Countenancecountenance, or a visible Lustrelustre or Brightnessbrightness of any Objectobject. The Imaginationimagination may be strongly impress'd with such things; but this is not spiritual Lightlight. Indeed when the Mindmind has a lively Discoverydiscovery of spiritual things, and is greatly affected by the Powerpower of divine Lightlight, it may, and probably very commonly doth, much affect the Imaginationimagination: Soso that Impressionsimpressions of an outward Beautybeauty or Brightnessbrightness, may accompany those spiritual Discoveriesdiscoveries. But spiritual Lightlight is not that Impressionimpression upon the Imaginationimagination, but an exceeding different thing from it. Natural Menmen may have lively Impressionsimpressions on their Imaginationsimaginations; and we cant determine but that the Devildevil, who transforms himself into an Angelangel of Lightlight, may cause Imaginationsimaginations of an outward Beautybeauty, or visible Gloryglory, and of Soundssounds and Speechesspeeches, and other such Thingsthings; but these are Thingsthings of a vastly inferiourinferior Naturenature to Spiritualspiritual Lightlight.

3. THIS spiritual Lightlight is not the suggesting of any new Truthstruths, or Propositionspropositions not contain'd in the Wordword of GOD. This suggesting of new Truthstruths or Doctrinesdoctrines to the Mindmind, independent of any antecedent Revelationrevelation of those Propositionspropositions, either in Wordword or Writing, is Inspirationinspiration; such as the Prophetsprophets and Apostlesapostles had, and such as some Enthusiastsenthusiasts pretend to. But this spiritual Lightlight that I am speaking of, is quite a different thing from Inspirationinspiration: Itit reveals no new Doctrinedoctrine, it suggests no new Propositionproposition to the Mindmind, it teaches no new thing of GOD, or CHRIST, or another Worldworld, not taught in the Bible; but only gives a due Apprehensionapprehension of those things that are taught in the word of GOD.

4. 'TIS not every affecting Viewview that Menmen have of the Thingsthings of Religionreligion, that is this spiritual and divine Lightlight. Men by meer Principlesprinciples of Naturenature are capable of being affected with Thingsthings that have a special Relationrelation to Religionreligion, as well as other Thingsthings. A Personperson by meer Naturenature, for Instanceinstance, may be liable to be affected with the Storystory of JESUS CHRIST, and the sufferings he underwent, as well as by any other tragical Storystory: Hehe may be the more affected with it from the Interestinterest he conceives Mankindmankind to have in it: Yeayea he may be affected with it without believing it; as well as a Manman may be affected with what he reads in a Romance, or see's acted in a Stage Play. He may be affected with a lively and eloquent description of many pleasant things that attend the state of the Blessedblessed in Heavenheaven; as well as his Imaginationimagination be entertain'd by a romantick description of the pleasantness of Fairy Landland, or the like. And that common belief of the
truth of the things of Religionreligion, that Personspersons may have from Educationeducation, or otherwise, may help forward their affection. We read in Scripture of many that were greatly affected with things of a religious nature, who yet are there represented as wholly graceless, and many of them very ill Menmen. A Personperson therefore may have affecting views of the things of Religionreligion, and yet be very destitute of spiritual Lightlight. Flesh and Bloodblood may be the Authorauthor of this: Oneone Manman may give another an affecting view of divine things with but common assistance; but GOD alone can give a spiritual Discoverydiscovery of them.
BUT I proceed to show,
Secondly, Positively, WHATwhat this spiritual and divine Lightlight is.
AND it may be thus described, A true sense of the divine Excellencyexcellency of the things revealed in the Wordword of GOD, and a conviction of the truth and reality of them, thence arising.

THIS spiritual Lightlight primarily consists in the former of these, viz. aA real sense and apprehension of the divine Excellencyexcellency of things revealed in the Wordword of GOD. A spiritual and saving Convictionconviction of the truth and reality of these things, arises from such a sight of their divine Excellencyexcellency and Gloryglory, so that this Convictionconviction of their truth is an effect and natural consequence of this sight of their divine Gloryglory. There is therefore in this spiritual Lightlight,

1. A true sense of the divine and superlative excellency of the things of Religionreligion; a real sense of the excellency of GOD, and JESUS CHRIST,
and of the work of Redemptionredemption, and the ways and works of GOD revealed in the Gospelgospel. There is a divine and superlative Gloryglory in these things; an Excellencyexcellency that is of a vastly higher Kindkind, and more sublime Naturenature, than in other things; a Gloryglory greatly distinguishing them from all that is earthly and temporal. He that is spiritually enlightened truly apprehends and sees it, or has a sense of it. He don't meerly rationally believe that GOD is Glorious, but he has a sense of the Gloriousness of GOD in his Heartheart. There is not only a rational belief that GOD is holy, and that Holinessholiness is a good thing; but there is a sense of the Lovelinessloveliness of GOD'sGod's Holinessholiness. There is not only a speculatively judging that GOD is gracious, but a sense how amiable GOD is upon that Accountaccount; or a sense of the Beautybeauty of this divine Attributeattribute.

THERE is a twofold Understandingunderstanding or Knowledgeknowledge of Goodgood, that GOD has made the Mindmind of Manman capable of. The Firstfirst, that which is meerly speculative or no • tio • nal ▪ Asas when a Personperson only speculatively judges, that any thing is, which by the Agreement of Mankindmankind, is called Goodgood or Excellentexcellent, viz. thatThat which is most to general Advantageadvantage, and between which and a Rewardreward there is a suitableness; and the like. And the other is that which consists in the sense of the Heartheart: Asas when there is a sense of the Beautybeauty, Amiablenessamiableness, or Sweetnesssweetness of a thing; so that the Heartheart is sensible of Pleasurepleasure and Delightdelight in the presence of the Ideaidea of it. In the former is exercised meerly the speculative Facultyfaculty, or the Understandingunderstanding strictly so called, or as spoken of in Distinctiondistinction from the Willwill or Dispositiondisposition
of the Soulsoul. In the latter the Willwill, or Inclinationinclination, or Heartheart, are mainly concern'd.

THUS there is a Differencedifference between having an Opinio • nopinion that GOD is holy and gracious, and having a sense of the Lovelinessloveliness and Beautybeauty of that Holinessholiness and Gracegrace. There is a Differencedifference between having a rational Judgmentjudgment that Honeyhoney is sweet, and having a sense 〈◊〉 of its sweetness. A Manman may have the Former 〈◊〉 former, that knows not how Honeyhoney tasts; but a Ma • nman can't have the Latterlatter, unless he has an Ideaidea of the tast of Honeyhoney in his Mindmind. So there is a difference between believing that a Personperson is Beautifulbeautiful, and having a sense of his Beautybeauty. The Formerformer may be obtain'd by hear-say, but the Latterlatter only by seeing the Count • enancecountenance. There is a wide difference between meer speculative, rational Judging any thing to be excellent, and having a sense of its Sweetnesssweetness, and Beautybeauty. The Fo • rmerformer rests only in the Headhead, Speculationspeculation only is concern'd in it; but the Heartheart is concern'd in the Latterlatter. When the Heartheart is sensible of the Beautybeauty and Amiablenessamiableness of a Thingthing, it necessarily feels Pleasurepleasure in the Apprehensionapprehension. It is implied in a Personspersons being heartily sensible of the Lovelinessloveliness of a thing, that the Ideaidea of it is sweet and pleasant to his Soulsoul; which is a far different thing from having a rational Opinionopinion that it is excellent.

2. THERE arises from this sense of divine Excellencyexcellency of Thingsthings contain'd in the Wordword of GOD, a Convictionconviction of the Truthtruth and Realityreality of them: and that either indirectly, or directly.
First, Indirectly, and that two ways.
